blocks.text: But they will marvel at him like little birds that surround an owl. Accordingly Hesychius: Σπίζια· ὄρνεα ἅπαντα [Spizia; ornea hapanta]. Rightly, provided that his ὄρνεα [ornea] are ὀρνίθια [ornithia] or ὀρνιθάρια [ornitharia], that is, little birds, not birds. Thus the Arabic عصفور [ʿuṣfūr], although properly it means sparrow, nevertheless embraces many species of little birds. Damir: وهى انواع منها ما هو مطرب بصوته ومنها ما يعجب بصورته وحسنه والعصفور الصوار هو الذي يجيب اذا ادعي من الصرورة وعصفور الجنة وهو الخطاف والعصفور البيوت فان في طباعه اختلافا [wa-hiya anwāʿ minhā mā huwa muṭrib bi-ṣawtihi wa-minhā mā yuʿjib bi-ṣūratihi wa-ḥusnihi wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-ṣawwār huwa alladhī yujību idhā duʿiya min al-ṣarūra wa-ʿuṣfūr al-janna wa-huwa al-khuṭṭāf wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-buyūt fa-inna fī ṭibāʿihi ikhtilāfan] There are various species of sparrows: some please by the modulation of their voice; others are admirable for their appearance and form. And the sparrow called suar is the one that, when called, answers by chirping. And the sparrow of paradise is the swallow. And the house sparrow is the one that is quarrelsome by nature, etc. And further on: ومن انواعه عصفور الشوك واكثر ماواه السياج وزعم ارسطو ان بينه وبين الحمار عداوة [wa-min anwāʿihi ʿuṣfūr al-shawk wa-akthar maʾwāhu al-siyāj wa-zaʿama Arisṭū anna baynahu wa-bayna al-ḥimār ʿadāwa] Among its species is the sparrow of thorns, which mostly lives in thickets. Aristotle reports that there is mutual hatred between it and the ass. It is plain that the acanthis is meant, which some explain as the goldfinch, others as the siskin, others as the ligurinus. For of it the Philosopher writes in Hist. book 8, chapter 3: Τὰ δὲ τοιάδε ἀκανθοφάγα, ἀκανθὶς, θραυπίς· ἔτι ἡ καλουμένη χρυσομήτρις. Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκανθῶν νέμεται [Ta de toiade akanthophaga, akanthis, thraupis; eti hē kaloumenē chrysomētris. Tauta gar panta epi tōn akanthōn nemetai]. Gaza rendered this as follows: These seek thorns: the siskin or ligurinus, the goldfinch, and also the one called aurivittis. For all these live on thorns. And in book 9, chapter 1: Ὄνος δὲ, καὶ ἀκανθίδες πολέμιοι· αἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν βοητεύουσιν [Onos de, kai akanthides polemioi; hai men gar apo tōn akanthōn boēteuousin] (read [II, 724] βιοτεύουσιν [bioteuousin]), ὁ δὲ ἁπαλὰς οὔσας ἐσθίει τὰς ἀκάνθας [ho de hapalas ousas esthiei tas akanthas]: The ass and the acanthides are enemies: for they get their living from thorns, which the ass eats while they are still tender. And the Arabs rightly assign this bird to the sparrow kind. For the acanthis is the same as the acanthyllis, of which Hesychius says: Ἀκανθυλλίς· στρουθοῦ γένος [Akanthyllis; strouthou genos], Acanthyllis, a kind of sparrow. In French it is called serin; whether from the song of the Sirens, as Belon holds in the Ornithology, book 7, chapter 14. There follows in Damir: ومن انواعه القبرة والحسون والبلبل والصعوة والحمرة والعندليب والمكاكي والصافر والتنوط والوصع والابوبراقش [col. 148] والقبعة [wa-min anwāʿihi al-qubbara wa-l-ḥassūn wa-l-bulbul wa-l-ṣaʿwa wa-l-ḥumra wa-l-ʿandalīb wa-l-makākī wa-l-ṣāfir wa-l-tanawwuṭ wa-l-waṣaʿ wa-l-abū barāqish wa-l-qubaʿa] Also among its species are the kubbara (the crested lark), and the hassun (I do not find it elsewhere; it seems to be named from its beauty) ^{(1)}, and the bulbul (the nightingale), and the savva (a little bird with a red crown), and the hamra (a red species of lark), and the andalib (a species of bird similar to the nightingale), and the mechachi (plural of the singular مكا [mukkā] maccha, a bird named from its whistling), and the saphir (which also whistles all night long with its head bent down and its feet fastened to the tree), and the thenavvut (a little bird not unlike this one, named from the nest that it hangs from a tree), and the vvasa (the wren), and the abubarakis (a songbird with long neck and legs, and red, yellow, green and blue feathers, which repeatedly change their colours), and the kubaa (a variegated little bird that draws in its neck when afraid, whence its name). These are the birds that the Arabs assign to the sparrow kind. So too among the Hebrews, according to Kimchi in his Lexicon: הוא רב המין לפיכך כלל כל עוף בזה השם, The sparrow has many species: hence this name is applied to all birds.
